title: What angle does each equal part of a circle make?
description: A full turn of three hundred and sixty degrees is shared equally among the parts when a circle is cut into one, two, three, four, five, six, eight, nine, ten and twelve parts. Keeko's doubt, that more parts make bigger angles, is broken by comparing a slice of a two part circle with a slice of a twelve part circle.
teaching_notes: One idea: equal parts share the full turn equally, so the angle of one part is three hundred and sixty divided by the number of parts. Watch for children who think more parts means a bigger angle.

source: The circle has been divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10
video_script.why: The child finds the angle of one part of a circle cut into equal parts by dividing the full turn of three hundred and sixty degrees.
video_script.substitution: The book's circles divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12 equal parts.
video_script.anchor: the book's ten circles divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12 equal parts
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says more parts make bigger angles, because there are more of them. The full turn stays the same, so more parts means a thinner slice and a smaller angle, and the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The angles are three hundred and sixty, one hundred and eighty and one hundred and twenty degrees. Next come ninety, seventy two and sixty degrees. The last four are forty five, forty, thirty six and thirty degrees.

final_answer.spoken: three hundred and sixty, one hundred and eighty, one hundred and twenty, ninety, seventy two, sixty, forty five, forty, thirty six and thirty degrees

maths_rules: equal parts share the full turn of 360 degrees equally, so angle of one part = 360 / number of parts
the full turn stays 360 degrees, so more parts means a smaller angle for each part
video_script.design: One circle at a time is shown cut into the stated number of parts, with one part shaded and its angle written beside it. The row of ten answers is written only at the end.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: angle of one part = 360° ÷ number of parts; 1 part: 360° ÷ 1 = 360°; 2 parts: 360° ÷ 2 = 180°; 3 parts: 360° ÷ 3 = 120°; 4 parts: 360° ÷ 4 = 90°

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step one, the parts are equal, so they share three hundred and sixty degrees equally. Divide by the number of parts.
<bookmark mark='first'/>One part gives three hundred and sixty. Two parts give one hundred and eighty. Three give one hundred and twenty, and four give ninety.

<bookmark mark='vals'/>Five parts give seventy two. Six parts give sixty. Eight parts give forty five.

beats.on_screen: Step 4, check: put the parts back together; 12 × 30° = 360°; 9 × 40° = 360°; 5 × 72° = 360°

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step four, check by putting the parts back together. Twelve parts of thirty degrees make three hundred and sixty.
